rulings.reason: The instruction scores how much intermediate algebra is written out, which is a completeness/verbosity property of the write-up rather than which method the solver used; the same approach can be shown in one line or ten. Its upstream cause (a meticulous, careful writer) plausibly also produces more canonical and correct reasoning, so it is reported both ways.

The instruction keys on the presence of organizational markers ('Claim:', 'Lemma:') and proof blocks, a presentation template that any approach -- canonical or divergent -- can be dressed in. A judge scoring exactly this text would measure formatting convention, not approach identity, so it is a declared nuisance.

The instruction is a lexical detector for AoPS community slang ('troll', 'scuffed', 'overkill'), so it scores register and self-presentation rather than the method on the page; a canonical solution by a slang-using poster is penalized and a divergent one by a plain writer is not. The self-label is nonetheless sometimes caused by a genuinely non-standard approach, so it is flagged mixed.

Scoring whether the post asserts, hedges, or disowns its argument requires reading the epistemic status of the displayed reasoning, and a post that asks why its answer is wrong or reproduces another's argument to object to it is thereby evidence that the displayed derivation is not an endorsed solution matching the reference. This is evidence about whether the item takes the canonical approach at all, not a mere framing tell.

The instruction scores extra scope -- generalizations, bonus observations, 'further remarks' sections -- which is a thoroughness/effort trait orthogonal to which route the solution took to the requested answer. Solvers who generalize may also be more likely to use the standard rigorous method, so it is reported in both discounted and undiscounted readouts.
